n: Ahithophel gives a sharp military plan: let him take twelve thousand men and chase David that very night, before David can regroup.
Striking while David is exhausted, he would scatter his followers and kill only the king — a quick, focused strike to avoid civil war.

f.w: I will smite the king only

n: With David dead, the people would return to Absalom and the nation would be at peace — like a bride returning to her husband, as some ancient versions put it.

f.w: the man whom thou seekest is as if all returned
f.g: The death of one man (David) would bring everyone back.

n: Absalom and Israel’s elders like the plan. It probably would have worked.
But Absalom wants a second opinion and summons Hushai — David’s secret agent. This is the answer to David’s prayer in 2 Samuel 15:31.

f.w: Call now Hushai the Archite also

n: Absalom explains Ahithophel’s plan and asks Hushai whether they should follow it.
Hushai boldly contradicts the famous counselor, but tactfully: Ahithophel’s advice is just “not good at this time.”
He plays on Absalom’s fear: David and his men are hardened warriors, as fierce as a mother bear robbed of her cubs. A veteran like David won’t be caught sleeping among his troops.

f.w: a bear robbed of her whelps

n: David is surely hiding somewhere, Hushai warns. If Absalom’s forces suffer early losses, panic will spread among them.
Even the bravest of Absalom’s men would lose heart, knowing David’s reputation.
Hushai advises gathering a massive army from all Israel, with Absalom leading it personally — flattering his vanity and buying David time.

f.w: as the sand that is by the sea for multitude

n: With overwhelming numbers they would cover David like dew on the ground and leave no survivors — a grand and vivid picture designed to impress.
Even if David hides in a city, all Israel could drag it into a valley with ropes. The exaggeration appeals to Absalom’s pride.
Absalom and his men choose Hushai’s advice. The narrator reveals why: the Lord had arranged to defeat Ahithophel’s good counsel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.

f.w: the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel

n: Hushai immediately reports both plans to the priests Zadok and Abiathar.
He urges that David cross the Jordan tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind and follows Ahithophel’s plan.
The priests’ sons wait at a spring outside the city to avoid notice. A servant girl brings them the message, and they set off to David.

f.g: A spring just south of Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley.
A maidservant, servant girl (no negative meaning in KJV English).

n: A boy spots them and tells Absalom. The messengers hurry to a house in Bahurim and hide in a well in its courtyard.
The woman of the house covers the well and spreads grain over it, hiding the young men. The scene recalls Rahab hiding the spies.

f.g: Crushed grain, spread out as if to dry.

f.w: spread a covering over the well's mouth

n: When Absalom’s men come, she misdirects them, and they give up and return to Jerusalem.

f.g: The meaning of this Hebrew word is uncertain.

n: The messengers climb out and rush to warn David to cross the Jordan quickly.
David leads all his people across the Jordan during the night; by morning, not one is left behind.

When his advice is rejected, Ahithophel foresees Absalom’s defeat. He goes home, puts his affairs in order, and takes his own life. Many see a parallel with Judas, the trusted friend who betrayed Jesus and then hanged himself.
David reaches Mahanaim, east of the Jordan — the same town that was Ish-bosheth’s capital. Absalom crosses the Jordan with all Israel to pursue him.
Absalom makes his cousin Amasa army commander instead of Joab. Amasa is also related to David, which makes this a family civil war.

f.g: Not David’s wife Abigail, but his sister or half-sister.

n: Absalom’s army camps in Gilead, east of the Jordan.

f.g: The highland region east of the Jordan River.

n: At Mahanaim, three unexpected friends come to help David: an Ammonite prince, the man who once sheltered Mephibosheth, and an aged wealthy Gileadite.
They bring bedding, bowls, pottery, and all kinds of grain and beans — generous supplies for weary refugees.

f.g: Lentils, beans, and other edible seeds.

n: They also bring honey, curds, sheep, and cheese, recognizing that David’s people were hungry, tired, and thirsty. In his darkest hour, God sends David friends.

f.g: Kine = cows; cheese from cows’ milk.
